common_name: Double Take Pink Flowering Quince (Thornless Double-Flowered Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Double Take Pink is a sibling to Double Take Orange, sharing the same thornless, essentially fruitless breeding.

directions: Double Take Pink bears fully double, ruffled, camellia-like flowers in soft pink, opening directly on bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, and like its Double Take series siblings was bred to be thornless, unlike the sharply spined branches of traditional flowering quince. Because the flowers are fully double and largely sterile, the shrub sets little to no fruit, putting its energy into the showy bloom display and making it easier to handle for pruning or cutting for arrangements without the scratches typical of older quince cultivars. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next season's flower buds.

common_name: Double Take Scarlet Flowering Quince (Thornless Double-Flowered Red Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Double Take Scarlet is the deep red-flowered member of the thornless, essentially fruitless Double Take quince series.

directions: Double Take Scarlet produces fully double, ruffled, camellia-like flowers in a rich, saturated red, opening on bare stems in late winter into early spring before the foliage emerges, giving one of the boldest early-season color displays of any hardy shrub. Bred thornless like its Double Take series siblings, it lacks the sharp spines that make older flowering quince cultivars unpleasant to prune or work around, and its largely sterile double flowers mean little to no fruit forms, concentrating the plant's energy into bloom. It tolerates poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and needs very little care beyond pruning right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood and heavy pruning at other times removes the coming season's flowers.

common_name: Golden Guinea Kerria (Large Single-Flowered Japanese Rose)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Golden Guinea bears larger single flowers than the straight species, on the same bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes.

directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Golden Guinea is a single-flowered kerria selection bred for noticeably larger, more substantial golden-yellow blooms than the species type, opening in mid-spring along bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes that provide subtle winter interest after leaf drop. Like other kerria it tolerates considerably more shade than most flowering shrubs while still blooming reliably, making it a good choice for a woodland edge, foundation planting, or naturalized shrub border. It suckers moderately to form a colony over time; prune out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year to keep the planting vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Jet Trail Flowering Quince (Compact Spreading White Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Jet Trail is a low, spreading, thorny flowering quince with pure white flowers, useful for a low informal hedge or mass planting.

directions: Jet Trail bears clusters of pure white flowers opening on bare, thorny branches in late winter into early spring, on a low, spreading shrub that stays under 3 feet, considerably more compact than most flowering quince cultivars. Its low, wide habit suits mass plantings, low informal hedges, and banks where a spreading rather than upright quince is wanted, and small yellow-green quince fruit follows the flowers in fall, edible for preserves though quite tart and hard raw. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, and drought-tolerant once its roots are settled. It blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing the following year's flower buds.
